questions.stem: Selling price is $40 and variable cost per unit is $22. What is contribution per unit?
whyNot: This adds the two figures.
This divides price by variable cost.
That is the variable cost, which is what you subtract.

questions.stem: Contribution per unit is $18 and 15,000 units are sold. Fixed costs are $180,000. What is profit?
whyNot: That is total contribution before fixed costs are deducted.
That is fixed costs, which is what you subtract.
This adds fixed costs instead of subtracting them.

questions.stem: Why are fixed costs usually irrelevant to a short-term special order decision?
options: They are paid whether or not the order is accepted, so they do not change as a result of the decision
Fixed costs do not exist in the short run
Fixed costs are always zero
Fixed costs are included in variable costs
questions.why: Only costs that change as a result of a decision are relevant to it. That is why the decision rests on contribution alone.
whyNot: They exist and are paid; they simply do not change with the decision.
They are usually substantial.
They are separate from variable costs.

questions.stem: A business normally sells at $40 with variable costs of $22. A customer offers $28 for 2,000 units and there is spare capacity. What should it do?
options: Accept: the order adds 2,000 x $6 = $12,000 of contribution
Reject: $28 is below the total cost per unit of $34
Reject: the price is below the normal selling price
Accept only if fixed costs are reduced first
questions.why: Fixed costs are already covered by existing sales and do not change, so the order adds $6 of contribution per unit. Using total cost per unit here is the error the topic exists to correct.
whyNot: Total cost per unit includes fixed costs that are paid either way, so it is the wrong basis.
A lower price is acceptable if it still exceeds variable cost, assuming spare capacity.
Fixed costs need not change for the order to be worthwhile.

questions.stem: What would reverse the decision to accept a low-price order?
options: If accepting it displaced full-price sales, losing $18 of contribution to gain $6
If the customer paid in advance
If fixed costs were lower than stated
If the order were larger
questions.why: Without genuine spare capacity the relevant comparison is what the order displaces. Checking capacity is the first evaluation point on any special order question.
whyNot: Earlier payment improves cash flow and strengthens the case.
Lower fixed costs would raise profit and not change the contribution logic.
A larger order adds more contribution, provided capacity exists.

questions.stem: Product X gives $30 contribution and uses 3 machine hours. Product Y gives $20 and uses 1 hour. Machine hours are scarce. Which should be made?
options: Y, because it gives $20 contribution per machine hour against X's $10
X, because its contribution per unit is higher
Both equally, because total contribution is the same
Neither, because contribution is too low
questions.why: With a limiting factor, rank by contribution per unit of the scarce resource. X gives 30/3 = $10 an hour; Y gives 20/1 = $20 an hour.
whyNot: Ranking by contribution per unit when a resource is scarce is the classic trap.
Per machine hour they differ by a factor of two.
Both have positive contribution and are worth making; the question is which first.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the best definition of a relevant cost?
options: A cost that changes as a result of a decision
A cost that has already been incurred
The total cost per unit of production
Any cost recorded in the accounts
questions.why: Only costs that change because of the decision should be considered in it. In a short-term decision with spare capacity, that means variable costs only.
whyNot: A cost already incurred is sunk and therefore irrelevant.
Total cost per unit includes irrelevant fixed costs.
Most recorded costs are irrelevant to any particular decision.

questions.stem: What is the main limitation of using contribution for decisions?
options: It is short term: in the long run fixed costs must be covered or the business fails
It cannot be calculated without fixed costs
It only applies to manufacturing
It always overstates profit
questions.why: A recurring low-price order becomes the price, and then the fixed costs are no longer covered. Contribution is the right tool for a one-off decision with spare capacity, not a pricing policy.
whyNot: Contribution per unit needs only price and variable cost.
It applies to services too.
It measures contribution accurately; the risk is applying it to the wrong kind of decision.

questions.stem: A product covers its variable costs but not its share of fixed costs. Why might the business keep it?
options: It still contributes towards fixed costs that would otherwise fall on other products
It is more profitable than the other products
Fixed costs disappear if a product is dropped
Variable costs would rise if it were dropped
questions.why: Dropping it removes its contribution, so the fixed costs it was helping to cover land on everything else. Total profit can fall as a result of dropping a seemingly loss-making product.
whyNot: It is less profitable; the point is that it still helps.
Fixed costs generally remain after a product is dropped.
Its own variable costs would disappear with it.
